html:
The sweet potato, a crop first grown in the Americas, reached China in the 1590s and spread widely under the Qing. It became one of the crops that let China's population grow so fast in the 1700s.

Spanish ships carried it across the Pacific to the Philippines on the Manila galleons. A Fujian merchant, Chen Zhenlong, is said to have smuggled vines out of Luzon in 1593. When famine struck Fujian in 1594, the provincial governor urged farmers to plant it, and it helped them survive.

The crop's great virtue was that it grew on poor, sandy or hilly land unfit for rice or wheat, and it gave many calories per field. With maize it let farmers move into hills and frontier land, feeding China's population surge from the late 1600s.

It was part of the wider Columbian Exchange. From China it spread to the Ryukyu Islands and Japan, where it helped people survive famines in the 1700s.
